questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance on a review board?
options: A review board should approve every AI use so no decision escapes oversight.
A review board should not approve every AI use, should not replace system owners, and should produce decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk.
A review board should be made up only of technologists so technical risk is fully understood.
A review board should replace the people who build, buy, own, and operate each AI system.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives three disciplines that keep a review board from becoming theater: it should not approve every AI use (that creates a bottleneck), it should not replace system owners (a named person stays accountable for each system), and a useful meeting produces decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk. A committee made of a single discipline, and a committee that does the building and owning, are presented as failures.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Frameworks overview - LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK”, what is the central focus?
options: By now you can build a single agent: a model, a loop, some tools. The hard part is deciding what holds the pieces together when the work grows.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: By now you can build a single agent: a model, a loop, some tools. The hard part is deciding what holds the pieces together when the work grows. This lesson surveys the five frameworks you will actually meet in the wild, and it is honest about what each one is for. LangChain is an integration ecosystem. LangGraph is a stateful graph runtime for workflows that branch and loop. CrewAI is a role-based layer for teams of agents with jobs and backstories. The OpenAI Agents SDK is a deliberately tiny set of primitives with clean handoffs and guardrails. The Claude Agent SDK gives the agent a computer with built-in file, shell, and edit tools. You will learn the mental model behind each one, see the same small task written in two of them so the difference is concrete, and finish with a decision path for choosing a framework instead of trusting star counts.

questions.explanation: The lesson says to write down the autonomous-versus-human boundary because it becomes the permissions model, and to define what a good run looks like so the test set is real tickets with known routes rather than a vibe check.

questions.question: What cost discipline does the lesson say keeps an eval quality gate from being switched off?
options: Run the full LLM-as-judge suite on every commit to catch regressions early
Use cheap code-based graders in CI on every commit and reserve expensive LLM-as-judge evaluations for preview and production
Run no automated evals and rely on manual review of a few prompts before each release
Run expensive evals only on Fridays so the bill stays low
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a gate costing real money on every commit gets switched off the first month, so it wires the cheap code-based layers into every-commit CI and reserves the expensive judges for preview and production evaluation.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance: Data Residency, Audit Logging, and Retention for AI Systems”, what is the central focus?
options: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders. Audit logging keeps an immutable record of what happened, per action, so a regulator or an investigator can reconstruct it later. Retention puts a clock on how long you keep any of it. This lesson reads the EU AI Act's record-keeping article and GDPR's storage-limitation principle, then shows how a real agent pipeline turns its own event stream into an auditable trail.

questions.question: How does the lesson say a capability eval becomes a regression eval?
options: A capability eval is deleted as soon as it passes so the suite stays small
A capability eval is refreshed from new production output each quarter
A capability eval that hits a persistently high pass rate graduates into the regression suite, where it starts measuring whether the behavior still works reliably
A capability eval is run only by human graders once it passes
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the self-healing structure: once an eval hits a persistently high pass rate it graduates from asking can we do this at all to asking can we still do this reliably, so nothing already proven can quietly regress.

questions.question: The lesson says a backup can meet the database RPO and still fail the retrieval RPO. What does that mean?
options: The database restore succeeded but the indexes were rebuilt with different ANN parameters
Rows were restored cleanly, but the retrieval system was not restored to a known semantic state, so search returns old chunks or mixes embedding model versions
The physical backup was taken before the last write was committed
The restore ran faster than the recovery time objective allowed
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: you restore the database cleanly, the application comes back, but support search returns old policy chunks and mixes two embedding model versions in the same result set. The backup met the database recovery point but failed the retrieval recovery point.

questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: An agent you cannot measure is an agent you cannot trust, and the moment a model changes you have no way to know what you traded away. This lesson walks the evaluation stack from the bottom up: the golden dataset that anchors everything, the classic metrics that break on open-ended output, the LLM-as-judge technique that replaces them, and the biases that make a judge lie, from position and verbosity preference to rating its own output too high and being misled by a confident wrong answer.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Workflow Automation Agents (Browsers, Clicks, and Typing)", what is the one idea to carry out?

Rules-based automation should be replaced entirely by agents
questions.explanation: The lesson states plainly that both failure modes in this class are engineering problems rather than prompting problems, and that both get solved before the agent ever runs in production.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Vector DB Operations: Scaling, Backups, Consistency, and Cost", what is the real variable that decides whether a pgvector HNSW index is fast?
options: The number of shards the collection is split across
Whether the index working set fits in memory, because HNSW traversal is a chain of random accesses and disk reads degrade latency by an order of magnitude or more
The PostgreSQL connection pool size

questions.explanation: The lesson states that HNSW search is a chain of random accesses through a graph and that the index must live in memory to be fast; when it spills to disk, query latency jumps 10 to 100 times. Row count is a proxy; memory is the variable.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about model risk management?
options: After the April 2026 replacement of SR 11-7 by SR 26-2, generative and agentic AI are carved out of supervisory scope, but the core discipline of inventory, tiering, independent validation, and ongoing monitoring still applies and must cover AI systems as models.
The US stopped requiring model risk management entirely in 2011, so AI systems no longer need any validation.
Model risk management applies only to banks and is irrelevant to how an enterprise decides which agents to run.
A model only needs to be validated once at launch and then requires no further monitoring because its risk profile never changes.
questions.explanation: The lesson confirms the April 2026 rescission of SR 11-7 in favor of SR 26-2 and notes that generative and agentic AI are excluded from the new guidance's scope, which means the hardest class of model must be governed by judgment for now. It then states the transferable core still holds for AI: inventory every system, tier by damage, validate high-risk systems independently, and monitor after deployment, since a model's risk profile changes as the world it operates in changes.

questions.explanation: The lesson opens by naming the three ways an agent breaks the code-determines-behavior assumption: the model, the prompts, and the retrieved data can each change without any application code changing.

questions.explanation: The lesson names those two risks specifically: the page can be adversarial input, and the agent's actions land in live systems rather than in a sandbox.

questions.question: Why should a web application firewall (WAF) not be treated as the only line of defense for an AI workload?
options: A WAF cannot enforce authentication or quotas on its own
A WAF reads the shape of requests, not their semantic meaning, so rephrased or encoded injections bypass string matching
A WAF costs more per evaluation than the model it protects
A WAF can only filter network traffic and never application-layer HTTP
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that a WAF reads text, not meaning, so an attacker can bypass a phrase match by rephrasing, encoding the prompt, or using indirect injection. That is why the semantic guardrail at the application layer is a second trust boundary.
